detail.longDescription: industrial ag mega-zine update: good news! both of my parents have signed off on my USSR pages. and i got my mom to write a very nice piece about her memories being a city girl who had to do seasonal labor on collective farms. i tried very hard on these pages... westerners get such flat images of the soviet union and i wanted to bring some life to the story... show that it was real people, not just stereotypes (poor babushkas, scary government officials, etc.) as a visual artist, the USSR offers a rich visual vernacular to play with. doing anything visual with a USSR theme is campy and full of possibilities. there are big, bold colors and graphics. very recognizable iconography. i didn't get to do as much of it as i'd like, because i'm trying to focus on text and photographs, but i still tried to include some propaganda posters, stamps (lots of great stamps: https:// commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Cat egory:Agriculture_of_the_Soviet_Union_on_stamps ), etc. mostly i wanted to get the story "right" in important ways. i think no one really knows everything that happened in soviet agriculture and why and how, but i wanted to convey enough of the story for people to come away with some of the major themes: the revolution was made by city people who didn't understand agriculture or rural people. stalin ruled for 30 years and it was a complete disaster: forced collectivization, famines, literal war on the peasants. after stalin, there were more good-faith (or perhaps "better-faith") efforts to improve agriculture, but it was always huge gambles, ramshackle implementation, massive fuckups, lack of input from people on the ground or agricultural scientists, and a hole that had already been dug so deep that it was probably impossible to make it work without overhauling the entire system of collective farms. anyway, now that the USSR pages are mostly done, i'm getting close to the end! i'm moving into the 1970s and the end of the thematic era that's the focus of the magazine: the high modernist period that praised scientific/industrial ag as the greatest thing since sliced bread (itself an invention of that time period). with oil crises, environmental problems, and failures of the grand promises of the green revolution, the dream of scientific ag lost some of its lustre, but the material reality of industrial agriculture just kept ramping up and up...it never went away and now here we are....... # agriculture # wip # USSR # AgriculturalHistory # research # history
